items.title: Practice Makes Perfect: Tacit Knowledge, Generative AI, and Returns to Schooling and Experience
items.desc: Using US CPS earnings data from 2018 to June 2026, the paper compares occupations by pre-ChatGPT AI exposure and finds the return to a year of schooling falls by 0.55 log points in exposed occupations after ChatGPT's release, while the experience profile rotates (up 0.26 at three years, down 0.12 at twenty-five). [arXiv econ.GN, submitted 2026-10-26]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today's paper asks a simple question with big stakes: if generative AI makes textbook-style knowledge cheap, what happens to the wage payoff from going to school, and the payoff from experience?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And the authors split human capital in two. Codified knowledge, the stuff you can write down and teach, versus practice-based knowledge, the judgment you build by doing the work.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Right. Their theory says AI substitutes for the codified part, so the return to schooling should fall. But if the two kinds of knowledge are complements, the return to experience should rise where people learn fastest by practice, early in a career.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: There's a twist, though. Some experience is tied to the old way of doing tasks, so it can become obsolete. That means the experience profile rotates rather than just shifting up or down.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: For data they use the US Current Population Survey earnings files from 2018 through June 2026. They compare occupations in the top and bottom quartiles of a pre-ChatGPT exposure index from Felten, Raj and Seamans, before and after ChatGPT's public release in November 2022.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So what did they find?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: After the release, the return to a year of schooling falls by 0.55 log points in exposed occupations. Against a pre-shock return of about 7.5 log points, that's roughly a seven percent decline.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And experience?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: It rotates. The return to a year of experience rises by 0.26 log points at three years of experience, shows no significant change at fifteen, and falls by 0.12 log points at twenty-five. In their baseline specification the effect crosses zero at about 18.1 years.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Do they check whether this is just something else going on?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They do. The breaks line up with the ChatGPT release, they disappear in a placebo using the pandemic date, they survive a common censoring rule, and they hold when each occupation gets its own pre-shock gradients.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Caveats: it's a difference-in-differences design that relies on parallel trends in those skill prices, and the exposure index is an occupation-level measure, so it isn't tracking individual AI use.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Takeaway: inside exposed occupations, codifiable knowledge is getting cheaper, and experience is worth more only if it transfers to the new technology. Human capital is being repriced, not just reduced.

items.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
items.desc: Combines a physics-informed neural network with a closed-form early-exercise projection to price American options with transaction costs, stochastic liquidity and two-factor stochastic volatility, matching finite-difference and Monte Carlo benchmarks. [arXiv q-fin.MF, submitted 2026-10-27]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This episode is based on the paper's abstract and early sections, so we'll keep it short. It's about pricing American options with deep learning.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: American options can be exercised early, which means you have to solve for the option value and the best exercise boundary at the same time. That's a free-boundary problem, and it's hard.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: It gets harder when you add realism. The authors include proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk whose drift they say is validated empirically on S and P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Put together, the pricing problem becomes a five-dimensional, highly nonlinear variational inequality. Grid-based methods struggle with that many dimensions.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Their approach is operator splitting. At each time layer, they split the problem into two parts: an elliptic continuation equation, approximated with a physics-informed neural network, and a closed-form projection step that enforces the early-exercise constraint.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So the neural net handles the diffusion part, and the early-exercise rule is handled exactly.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They also derive a conditional stability bound under stated assumptions, and they validate the scheme against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks. Prices and the learned exercise boundary agree closely with the reference solutions, and they run sensitivity analyses on the key parameters.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The limit here is that this is a numerical-methods paper; it shows the method works against benchmarks, not that it improves trading outcomes.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Takeaway: deep learning can make high-dimensional American option pricing tractable while keeping the early-exercise structure intact.

items.title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
items.desc: Adds 10-K-derived knowledge-graph context to finance LLMs at inference time, without retraining, to score news sentiment with explainable evidence; simulations show better portfolio performance than the baseline. [arXiv cs.CL, submitted 2026-10-26]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This episode is based on the abstract and introduction. The paper is FinLLM-KG, from Imperial College London, about financial sentiment analysis for algorithmic trading.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The problem is that current finance-tuned language models score each news article on its own, and they're black boxes. But news about one firm can matter for its competitors, suppliers and customers.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Their idea is to feed the model extra context at inference time, without retraining it. The context comes from a knowledge graph built from SEC 10-K filings, and it's supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a few relevance-ranked factual triples, like one company partners with another.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And there's a temporal gate, so only the latest 10-K filed strictly before the article is used. That avoids look-ahead.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: It works with any causal language model. The authors also attribute each sentiment score back to individual sentences and retrieved facts, so a human reviewer can inspect the evidence.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Does it make money in simulation?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The abstract says simulations show it consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline. We're working from the abstract here, so we won't quote specific numbers.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Caveat: those are simulated portfolios, so transaction costs and real-world implementation would need testing.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Takeaway: grounding sentiment scores in firm-level filings can make LLM trading signals both better informed and easier to audit.

briefing.text: Hello, this is the Daily AI Research Digest for October twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six. I'm Alex.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And I'm Sam. Today's theme: the money behind AI is getting a hard look, from debt markets to the Anthropic offering.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Let's start with a new arXiv paper on generative AI and wages. Using US earnings survey data through June twenty twenty-six, the authors compare occupations more and less exposed to AI, before and after ChatGPT's release.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: What do they see?

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The return to a year of schooling falls by about half a log point in exposed occupations, roughly seven percent of its earlier level. The return to experience rises early in a career, and turns negative after about eighteen years.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: So AI makes book knowledge cheaper, and experience is valuable mostly if it carries over to the new technology.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Now to finance. Bloomberg reports that Wall Street's AI debt machine is starting to choke on supply. Early signs suggest the credit market is approaching the limits of how much more debt it can absorb.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: That fits a Bloomberg story about a three point one billion dollar loan being syndicated by Zankore, an Nvidia-backed AI infrastructure firm in Indonesia, adding to the flurry of financing for Asia's buildout.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: And The Economist asks whether insurance would pay out in an AI blow-up, noting credit default swaps are back in vogue amid fears of a debt disaster.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Meanwhile, Microsoft and Alphabet report earnings, and Bloomberg says investors are focused on how heavy AI spending weighs on cash flow.

briefing.text: On the other side, SK Hynix reported better than expected quarterly operating profit, and the FT says it will return seventy-five billion dollars to investors this year.

briefing.text: Then there's Anthropic. The New York Times says Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are competing for the top bank role in its public offering, and the Wall Street Journal describes how Anthropic's market opportunity estimate is tied to the value of knowledge workers' output.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: The Journal also reports Anthropic describing enterprise adoption as still in the early phases, which is a notable thing to say alongside a giant offering.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: On finance methods, there's a paper from Imperial College on FinLLM-KG. It feeds company facts from annual filings into a language model at inference time to score news sentiment, and reports better simulated portfolio performance than a baseline.

briefing.text: And a deep learning paper prices American options with transaction costs, liquidity risk and stochastic volatility, matching standard benchmarks.
